hero.headline: St. Lucie County wrongful death lawsuit filed after Florida Turnpike crash killed three workers
hero.teaser: Angeline Dowdian filed a wrongful death lawsuit against a truck driver and his company after a crash on the Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County killed her mother and two others in August 2025.
hero.body:
On August 12, 2025, a minivan carrying three workers became wedged underneath a semi-truck on the Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County. The truck's driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly made an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. Faniola Joseph, 37, Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, all died in the crash. Joseph had been traveling south from Indiana to purchase goods for her retail business. Now her daughter, 22-year-old Angeline Dowdian, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, his employer White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson.

The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly hired White Hawk Carriers despite the company's serious safety violations. Attorney Dax Bello of Stuart represents Angeline and argues this was not a random accident but a foreseeable consequence of unsafe practices. "This is not an accident. It's a predictable end that came at the cost of three lives," Bello said. The case gains strength from a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when they place unsafe drivers on the road. Transportation expert James Lewis has described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." Bello emphasizes that brokers and carriers have a responsibility to check publicly available safety records before putting drivers on the road.

Angeline lived abroad and had not seen her mother in six years, though they spoke daily through video calls. When the crash occurred, she missed a call from her mother. "She sent me a voice message. She said, 'Angeline, where are you?' This is the first message I go to every morning," Angeline said. She described losing her mother as losing everything. Her father had rejected her at birth, making her mother both parents to her. Visa restrictions have prevented her from visiting her mother's grave since the crash.

Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warned the company may reopen under a different name, a practice he said is common in the industry. Angeline's co-counsel Mark Brumer added that litigation will address not only who caused the crash but who could have prevented it. While no legal victory will undo her pain, Angeline hopes the lawsuit prevents other families from suffering as hers has. "I don't want nobody suffer like me," she said. "She worked her whole life so I could have a better one, and died in such a terrible way."

cards.headline: Indian River County could lose $50 million under property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.teaser: Indian River County leaders warned Friday that a property tax amendment on the November ballot could cost the county $50 million in annual revenue by 2028.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss a property tax amendment appearing on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Vice Chair Laura Moss and other county officials warned that the measure could cost the county approximately $50 million in annual revenue by 2028. Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called it "an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy." Moss criticized the state for imposing the amendment on local governments, saying "They've declared war on local government" and emphasizing that "Every county is different. We fund what the community wants."

With a budget of around $597 million, the projected $50 million loss represents a significant portion that cannot be replaced without impacting essential services. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, potentially affecting three projected stations. Approximately 79.1% of fire rescue funding comes from ad valorem taxes. Lunceford described the amendment as "less of a tax cut, and more of a tax shift," warning that the county may raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties, increase impact fees, or raise utility fees to offset the lost revenue.

cards.headline: 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide after Fort Pierce shooting leaves another teen critically injured
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old faces an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce that left another 16-year-old in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. Detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered lying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds. Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects, with one caught by a sheriff's office K9 and another found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene.

The 16-year-old victim remains in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning, according to Fort Pierce police. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

cards.headline: DeSantis joins calls for Florida GOP governor debate as party excludes candidate from June event
cards.teaser: Gov.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis joined several candidates Friday in calling for a public debate after the Republican Party of Florida announced its June 27 Sunshine State Showdown in Hollywood will not include a full debate. The party set three qualification benchmarks: at least 10% polling support, more than $10 million raised and more than 10,000 donors. Only U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican front-runner, met all three thresholds. The party's June 9-10 poll showed Donalds leading with 38.8% support, followed by Jay Collins at 7.6%, businessman James Fishback at 4.1% and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2.2%. Nearly 43% remained undecided. DeSantis criticized the criteria, saying he would not have qualified under these standards when he ran in 2018, and argued debates should be arranged by candidates and media organizations rather than party officials.

Renner and Collins both called for a debate, with Collins launching a website and petition. Donalds' campaign dismissed the pressure, with communications director Gates McGavick stating there are no participation trophies in politics and it is not Donalds' job to legitimize unsuccessful campaigns. The Florida GOP rescinded Fishback's invitation to the Sunshine State Showdown after he announced a competing July 15 debate, saying participation in unsanctioned events violated party rules. Party Chairman Evan Power also accused Fishback of antisemitic and racist attacks against party members. The primary is scheduled for August 18.

"I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," Enrique said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity." His accomplishment represents both his personal dedication and his role as a role model and change-maker in his community.

Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, emphasized that while Enrique's achievement is historic, his character stands out most. Enrique has shown the ability to turn obstacles into advantages and support others with both humility and determination. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and an experienced Youth of the Year judge, noted that Enrique impressed judges from the beginning. "From the start, Enrique stood out," Leonard said. "Thanks to his hard work and all those who support him, we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community."

Enrique's family expressed deep gratitude for his success. His parents said they are thankful to God for the opportunities their son has received and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for supporting his growth as both a leader and a person. As he prepares for his next chapter, Enrique will attend the University of Florida this fall while competing for the national Youth of the Year title. His journey from a non-English speaking newcomer to valedictorian and regional award winner demonstrates the power of perseverance, community support, and opportunity.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Pride memorial proposal stalled by new state law restricting DEI funding
cards.teaser: A proposed rainbow pyramid monument to honor Pulse nightclub victims in Delray Beach faces delays due to Senate Bill 1134, which would ban local governments from funding diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. The Pride intersection mural was sandblasted away by the state in 2025.
cards.body:
A proposal to build a rainbow pyramid monument in Delray Beach to honor victims of the Pulse nightclub massacre has stalled due to Senate Bill 1134, which awaits the governor's decision. The bill would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. It passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House. The measure could put state funding at risk if municipalities use city property or dollars for such projects. Commissioner Juli Casal said the city must work within the parameters of the law because it relies heavily on state funding.

The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee formed by March and designed a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color, illuminated at night. Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer proposed placing it at Old School Square near the Eagle Scout monument, steps from where a Pride mural once stood. The original Pride intersection mural, which honored Pulse victims, was sandblasted away by the Florida Department of Transportation in August 2025 to comply with statewide regulations removing political and ideological messaging. Casal said if private funding and private property could be found, the process might accelerate. Dunayer said she is reaching out to state leaders and national organizations to find solutions and believes the memorial is important to honor those who gave their lives.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County man charged with vehicular homicide after I-95 crash killed 92-year-old Boynton Beach woman
cards.teaser: Guy Augustin was arrested Wednesday and charged with vehicular homicide eight months after a crash on Interstate 95 in Boynton Beach killed Martha Gutierrez, who was three days from her 93rd birthday.
cards.body:
Guy Augustin, 22 at the time of the collision, faces a vehicular homicide charge eight months after a crash on Interstate 95 in Boynton Beach killed Martha Gutierrez on October 8, 2025. The two-vehicle wreck occurred at approximately 9:45 p.m. on southbound I-95 just south of the Gateway Boulevard exit. According to a probable cause affidavit, Augustin was driving a 2013 BMW 535i when he changed lanes improperly, moving behind Gutierrez's Toyota Camry and striking her vehicle in the rear. The impact sent Gutierrez's car into a concrete barrier wall and Augustin's BMW off the road into the grass. Gutierrez was transported to Delray Medical Center but was pronounced dead at 11:22 p.m. Gutierrez was three days away from her 93rd birthday.

Investigators said Augustin admitted to traveling at speeds of 95-100 mph in a 65 mph speed zone and was following two motorcycles too closely before the collision. A witness told investigators that Augustin passed her at a high rate of speed while weaving in and out of traffic at approximately 80 mph. FHP investigators downloaded data from the BMW showing the vehicle traveled at 123 mph, then 119 mph until impact where the speed registered at 117 mph. Event Data Recorder data indicated the impact speed was between 111.24 and 132.41 mph. Augustin, who lives near West Palm Beach, is being held at the Palm Beach County jail on a $100,000 bond.

hero.headline: Wellington tops Palm Beach County rent at $2,850 for one-bedroom while Belle Glade offers cheapest at $890
hero.teaser: Wellington ZIP code 33449 posted the highest Fair Market Rent rates in Palm Beach County, with one-bedroom apartments reaching nearly $2,850 monthly, while Belle Glade offers the county's most affordable rental market.
hero.body:
Wellington residents face the highest rental costs in Palm Beach County, with Fair Market Rent reaching nearly $2,850 for a one-bedroom apartment, according to 2026 data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. ZIP code 33449 in Wellington posted four-bedroom homes exceeding $5,080 monthly, while Belle Glade offers the county's most affordable rental market at $890 for comparable housing. Luis Rivera, who lives in Section 8 housing in Palm Beach County, said rent prices were normal when he first arrived but now exceed two or three thousand dollars even in unreasonable neighborhoods. Joanne Bromfield recently relocated from Tampa after a 12-year education career and switched to real estate. She found the Palm Beach County rental market surprisingly expensive, walking away from signing a lease just minutes before speaking with media.

Real estate broker Talbot Sutter, president of Sutter and Nugent Real Estate, attributes Wellington's high costs to quality school districts and lifestyle amenities including equestrian activities and outdoor recreation. Sutter works with high-end clients, often executives from New York City, who rent luxury properties before purchasing. He identifies the priciest rental markets as Wellington, western Lake Worth, Delray Beach and Boca Raton, noting that more acreage and land has become popular even for rentals. HUD's Fair Market Rent data helps calculate housing assistance programs but does not set rent control limits for landlords.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses Stuart thrift stores to house cats during Palm City shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast shifted many of its cats to two thrift store locations after beginning construction on adoption, customer service, and intake areas at its Palm City shelter earlier this year.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to maintain animal care during a major renovation of its Palm City shelter, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily shifting many of its cats to store locations. With shelter cages unavailable during the renovation, the stores have become a lifeline for the animals, Fisher said.

Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats alongside unique items for sale at both thrift stores. Every purchase helps provide for the animals, Ellis noted, and the organization welcomes donations of gently used goods. The Humane Society is also currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Hundreds of dead fish found in Port St. Lucie's Sawgrass Lakes after city algae treatment
cards.teaser: Dead fish were floating in the Sawgrass Lakes community in Port St. Lucie on Thursday, after the city hired a vendor to treat the water for algae earlier in the week.
cards.body:
Dead fish were floating on the water at Sawgrass Lakes in Port St. Lucie on Thursday morning after the city hired SOLitude to treat the water for algae on Tuesday and Wednesday. Neighbors found hundreds of dead fish in their backyards and shared videos with WPTV. "There were hundreds and hundreds of fish here, and thousands of those little ones just gulping the air," said neighbor Jim Herbert. Experts told WPTV that with high heat and algae treatment combined, the water can become uninhabitable for aquatic life. On Thursday, crews removed the dead fish and tested oxygen levels in the water.

Jim Herbert said this is at least the second fish die-off since he has lived in the community. Scott Samples with the city of Port St. Lucie said they have been working with neighbors and other cities and counties to find solutions, hoping that a couple of options might be available soon. Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, said the city should look at more natural solutions like planting aquatic vegetation, reducing fertilizer use, and removing sediment that can fuel algae growth. "We're going to end up in a cycle that we can't break unless we go back to square one and start with a natural remediation," Moir said.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss from property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose around $50 million from its $597 million budget if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot, county leaders.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to warn that the county could lose around $50 million from its $597 million budget if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Laura Moss, vice chair of the Indian River County Commission, said the state is dictating to local governments how they fund services. Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called the amendment less of a tax cut and more of a tax shift.

According to county officials, the $50 million loss would significantly impact local services. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, with 79.1% of funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Three projected fire stations may not happen if the shortfall occurs. Lunceford warned that the county cannot fill a hole that size without cutting into law enforcement and first responder services. He said the amendment could force the county to raise impact fees, utility fees, or increase taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit in Fort Pierce invites visitors to explore Florida coastal habitats
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce displays fully live, complex models of ecosystems dating back to 1980 under the Smithsonian.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman said the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. The facility houses more species than many larger exhibits. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating intricate relationships between organisms. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran said the touch tank is a crowd favorite where guests can handle unusual marine species under staff guidance.

The facility operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced by live displays. The facility is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information can be found at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year.

cards.headline: Governor DeSantis announces Medicaid fraud crackdown in West Palm Beach targeting fake providers
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced new Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday in West Palm Beach, revealing that more than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers were actually staged operations created solely to steal from the state program.
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis announced sweeping Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday at the Health Care District of Palm Beach County in West Palm Beach, targeting criminal operations that have cost Florida taxpayers millions. Agency for Healthcare Administration Secretary Shevaun L. Harris revealed that more than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers in West Palm Beach were actually staged operations created solely to steal from the state program. DeSantis said southeast Florida is one of the fraud hotspots in the United States, noting that while Palm Beach County has significant fraud issues, Miami-Dade and Broward counties are even worse.

The state announced three major initiatives to combat fraud: a pilot program with Ventolin, an identity fraud detection company specializing in uncovering sophisticated schemes; enrollment moratoriums on high-risk provider categories including durable medical equipment suppliers and adult day care providers; and a comprehensive revalidation effort requiring all active Florida Medicaid providers to verify credentials. Harris said Florida's program integrity efforts have already saved $136.45 million in recovery and prevention benefits, and over the past two years AHCA has terminated or denied enrollment to more than 3,200 providers. DeSantis credited the Trump administration and Dr. Mehmet Oz at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for supporting the initiative.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at St. Lucie County Aquarium showcases Florida's ocean habitats in Fort Pierce
hero.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium offers rare close-up encounters with marine life at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce is home to a unique marine exhibit that stands out among public aquariums across the country. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates with a distinctive philosophy that sets it apart from typical facilities. According to Manager Bill Hoffman, the aquarium has been displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems since 1980 under Smithsonian direction. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said, noting that the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits. The partnership between the St. Lucie County Aquarium and the Smithsonian Marine Station allows visitors to explore Florida's most important coastal environments in one location.

The centerpiece of the exhibit is the Atlantic coral reef tank, a large display that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Beyond the coral reef, visitors can observe live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities. Each habitat demonstrates the complex relationships between different organisms that depend on one another for survival. Even smaller creatures play crucial roles in these ecosystems, as evidenced by displays featuring animals like a four-inch barracuda. These exhibits work together to tell the story of Florida's marine biodiversity and the delicate balance required to maintain healthy ocean environments.

One of the most popular attractions is the touch tank, where guests can handle unusual marine species under the supervision of trained staff members. According to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran, visitors often encounter animals they have never seen before in this hands-on area. This interactive experience helps connect people directly to marine life and creates memorable educational moments. The facility plans to expand its programming as part of its 25th anniversary celebration happening later this year.

The aquarium's mission extends beyond entertainment and education. By showcasing these live ecosystems, the facility aims to raise public awareness about threats to ocean health while inspiring conservation efforts. Manager Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on countless small organisms working together, a message reinforced through the live displays throughout the exhibit. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and welcomes visitors year-round. For more information, visit sms.si.edu or check their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Curaçao's World Cup soccer team trains in Boca Raton, draws fans from Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday to watch Curaçao prepare for its first-ever World Cup appearance th.
cards.body:
Hundreds of soccer fans gathered at Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday, waving jerseys and flags as Curaçao's national team prepared for its first-ever World Cup appearance. The training session drew enthusiastic supporters from across South Florida, including some who traveled as far as Port St. Lucie. Goalkeeper Eloy Room told WPTV that the crowd's energy has fueled the team's excitement for the tournament. "Really joyful to see that so many people showed up today — it gives us energy. We're really excited to start the World Cup," Room said. Midfielder Tahitch Chong expressed the significance of the moment for the island nation. "I think it's amazing to see. I don't think the people back home are going to believe the crowd we had here," Chong said.

Curaçao, an island nation with just over 150,000 people, is the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament and went undefeated through all 10 of its 2026 World Cup qualifying matches. Fan Marionella Barzeycoggins, originally from Curaçao, brought her entire family to the event after learning about the training session. Local supporter Bruce Zalman said the atmosphere was incredible and expressed hope to attend upcoming games at the Hard Rock. Curaçao faces Germany this Sunday in Houston, Texas.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses thrift stores in Stuart to house cats during Palm City shelter renovation

"With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said. cards.headline: Palm Beach County deputy cites Lake Worth woman for holding phone in hand she was born without
cards.teaser: Body camera footage from a traffic stop shows a deputy accusing Katie Thomas of holding a phone in her right hand while driving. Thomas was born without a right hand.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Lake Worth resident Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving, unaware that Thomas was born without a right hand. Body camera footage shows the deputy telling Thomas, "You drove past me, holding the phone with your right hand, manipulating that phone." When Thomas raised her arm to show her stump, the deputy continued questioning whether she had her phone in hand. The traffic stop has generated 110 million views on social media, with Thomas telling media that "literally being accused of something that I did not have a limb to be accused" made the violation immediately apparent as impossible to 110 million people.

The citation was dropped for lack of evidence. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review of the case is underway. Thomas, an adaptive athlete who has raised awareness for the limb-difference community, said she harbors no ill will toward the sheriff's office and would be open to a conversation about using the moment to spread awareness. She has started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on her Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital. Thomas said she has no plans to sue and hopes the attention helps people understand the limb difference community.

cards.headline: Delray Beach fights state restrictions to create memorial honoring Pulse victims 10 years after massacre
cards.teaser: Friday marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando. A rainbow-painted Pride intersection in Delray Beach that honored the 49 victims was sandblasted away by the state last year.
cards.body:
In August 2025, Delray Beach leaders challenged state pressure to remove a rainbow-painted Pride mural honoring Pulse victims, arguing it sat on city property rather than state roads. The Florida Department of Transportation sandblasted away the mural within weeks to comply with a statewide effort to regulate road markings and remove political and ideological messaging. Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents formed the Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee to create an alternative. By March, they designed a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color, to be illuminated at night and placed at Old School Square near the Eagle Scout monument.

Two major obstacles now block the project: using city money for the memorial and placing it on city land. Commissioner Juli Casal cited Senate Bill 1134, which passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House and awaits the governor's decision, as a fresh legal barrier. The bill would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, potentially putting state funding at risk. Casal stated that private funding and private property could allow the project to move forward immediately.

cards.headline: Gov. Ron DeSantis announces Medicaid fraud crackdown in West Palm Beach targeting Southeast Florida
cards.teaser: DeSantis announced sweeping new Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday afternoon in West Palm Beach, targeting criminal operations concentrated in Southeast Florida.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced sweeping Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday afternoon at the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, partnering with President Donald Trump's administration and federal agencies to combat fraud concentrated in Southeast Florida. DeSantis noted that while fraud affects Miami-Dade and Broward counties as well, Southeast Florida remains a significant fraud hotspot in the United States. Agency for Healthcare Administration Secretary Shevaun L. Harris revealed that more than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers in West Palm Beach were actually staged operations created solely to steal from the state program. Investigators discovered the fake operations through shared addresses across multiple unrelated entities, suspicious ownership structures, and no evidence of actual patient care.

The state announced three major initiatives to combat fraud. First, AHCA is launching a pilot program with Ventolin, an identity fraud detection company that identifies stolen IDs, synthetic IDs, and hidden ownership structures. Second, AHCA has imposed enrollment moratoriums on high-risk provider categories including durable medical equipment suppliers and adult day care providers. Third, the state is requiring all active Florida Medicaid providers to verify their credentials and identity, with non-responsive providers removed from the program. Florida's program integrity efforts have already saved $136.45 million in recovery and prevention benefits, and over the past two years, AHCA has terminated or denied enrollment to more than 3,200 providers.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Public Library offers free STREAM summer programs with daily lunches for youth
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Public Library is making summer brighter for kids and teens with free STREAM programs in Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math, open to all Florida residents.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free STREAM summer programs — Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math — to all Florida residents. Natalie Baron, young adult librarian, is leading sessions like ColorSpace: Artistic Excavations, where teens explore art history from cave paintings to ancient pottery. Teens can also join lab-based activities, including collaborative 3D puzzle builds, and pick up themed book boxes. Mandy Fulop, head of the children's department, is launching the STREAM Into Summer Literacy Program, encouraging readers to set goals with librarians, track progress, and take home an Unearth a Story bag with a free STREAM book and activities. Family Nights on select Tuesdays invite children 5 and older to explore STREAM topics together. Saturday Science Discovery programs for ages 9 to 12 feature hands-on archaeology activities such as "Piece Together History," trash bag archaeology, carbon dating, and fossil hunts. Registration is available at delraylibrary.org.

In partnership with the School District of Palm Beach County, the library serves free lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and snacks from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m., to youth up to 18. Upcoming Thursday guests include Malachi Fenn from the Florida Public Archaeology Network on June 11, Sea Turtle Adventures beach cleanup on June 25, American Shark Conservancy's SharkSmarts on July 2, and FPAN Beyond Artifacts on July 16. A full program lineup and registration details are available at delraylibrary.org.

hero.headline: Eleven Republicans qualify for crowded race to succeed Byron Donalds in Congress
hero.teaser: With Byron Donalds running for Governor, Florida's 19th Congressional District will host the most crowded field of congressional candidates in the state, including two former Congressmen who previously represented other states.
hero.body:
Florida's 19th Congressional District is shaping up to have the most crowded field of congressional candidates in the state following Byron Donalds' decision to run for Governor. With qualification deadlines now closed, the Republican Primary includes 11 candidates competing for the open seat. This represents an even larger field than the last time the district held an open race, when 10 Republican candidates qualified. Donalds himself emerged from that previous primary before winning the 2020 General Election.

The Republican field includes two former members of Congress who previously served other states: Madison Cawthorn and Chris Collins. Major self-funders in the race are Jim Oberweis, a dairy farm owner and former Illinois lawmaker, and Jim Schwartzel, president of Sun Broadcasting. Other notable candidates include author and health activist Catalina Lauf and former congressional staffer Ola Hawatmeh. Veteran Mike Pedersen also qualified for the ballot, along with Greg "Tex" Bukowski, a Sarasota County Charter Review Board member, and Linda Sawyer, a former researcher at the National Institutes of Health. January 6 insurrectionist John Strand rounds out the GOP Primary ballot.

The Democratic Primary features three candidates. Howard Sapp, a former state House candidate and air traffic controller, and Victor Arias, managing attorney of Arias Law Firm, qualified for the ballot. Robert Neeld, who has previously challenged former GOP Representatives Connie Mack IV and Rooney, also made the Democratic Primary ballot shortly before the deadline. Additionally, Seth Haskin qualified to run without party affiliation and will face whichever candidates prevail in both primaries during the general election in November. A write-in candidate, Alexandra Zakhvatayev, also qualified in the race.

The winner of the Republican Primary in August will enter the general election as a heavy favorite in this heavily Republican district. Under the new congressional map enacted by Governor Ron DeSantis, more than 69 percent of voters in the district voted for Republican Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election, while just 34 percent backed Democrat Kamala Harris. This significant Republican advantage suggests the August primary winner will likely win the seat in November's general election.

cards.headline: DeSantis extends Independence Day holiday for Florida state workers to mark America 250
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Friday that state offices will be closed on Thursday, July 2, and Monday, July 6, giving Florida's 100,000 state employees additional time off to celebrate the nation's 250th anniversary.
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis announced Friday that state offices will be closed on Thursday, July 2, 2026, and Monday, July 6, 2026, giving Florida's 100,000 state employees additional time off to celebrate America's 250th anniversary. "America's 250th anniversary is a historic milestone and an opportunity to reflect on the courage, sacrifice, and enduring principles that established the United States as the freest and most prosperous nation in the world," DeSantis said.

The governor framed the extended holiday as part of Florida's leadership in the semiquincentennial celebration. "As Florida leads the nation's semiquincentennial celebration, I am pleased to provide state employees additional time to celebrate our country's founding, participate in America 250 events, and spend time with family and friends honoring the blessings of liberty that generations of Americans have fought to preserve," DeSantis added. As part of the celebration, DeSantis has focused on procuring statues of historic figures for display throughout the state, many of them American Presidents. He has frequently cited the Founding Fathers in speeches, particularly Benjamin Franklin's statement after the ratification of the Constitution that the country was a Republic, if you can keep it. DeSantis has also said Florida was the 14th colony at various points, framing the celebration as a way to remind Floridians of the Sunshine State's unique role from the beginning of the Republic.

cards.headline: DeSantis joins calls for Florida GOP governor debate as party excludes candidate from June event
cards.teaser: Gov.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis joined several candidates Friday in calling for a public debate after the Republican Party of Florida announced its June 27 Sunshine State Showdown in Hollywood will not include a full debate. The party set three qualification benchmarks: at least 10% polling support, more than $10 million raised and more than 10,000 donors. Only U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican front-runner, met all three thresholds. The party's June 9-10 poll showed Donalds leading with 38.8% support, followed by Jay Collins at 7.6%, businessman James Fishback at 4.1% and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2.2%. Nearly 43% remained undecided. DeSantis criticized the criteria, saying he would not have qualified under these standards when he ran in 2018, and argued debates should be arranged by candidates and media organizations rather than party officials.

Renner and Collins both called for a debate, with Collins launching a website and petition. Donalds' campaign dismissed the pressure, with communications director Gates McGavick stating there are no participation trophies in politics and it is not Donalds' job to legitimize unsuccessful campaigns. The Florida GOP rescinded Fishback's invitation to the Sunshine State Showdown after he announced a competing July 15 debate, saying participation in unsanctioned events violated party rules. Party Chairman Evan Power also accused Fishback of antisemitic and racist attacks against party members. The primary is scheduled for August 18.

cards.headline: Ten candidates qualify for race to succeed Frederica Wilson in Florida's 24th Congressional District
cards.teaser: A race to replace longtime Democratic U.S. Rep. Frederica Wilson features seven Democrats, including Miami-Dade County Democratic Party Chair Shevrin Jones and Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert.
cards.body:
Ten candidates qualified to compete for Florida's 24th Congressional District seat vacated by longtime Democratic U.S. Representative Frederica Wilson. The race features seven Democrats, one Republican, one candidate with no party affiliation, and a write-in candidate. The district, which covers Miami Gardens in Miami-Dade County and Hollywood, Miramar and Pembroke Park in Broward County, is deeply blue, making the Democratic primary winner the likely November victor.

Shevrin Jones, Chair of the Miami-Dade County Democratic Party and former Senate Democratic Leader prospect, leads the Democratic field. Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert, a former Mayor of Miami Gardens and immediate past Chair of the County Commission, is also a major contender who raised $250,000 in his first five days of campaigning. Other Democrats include Kendrick Meek Jr., son and grandson of former congressional members; Miami-Dade Commissioner Jean Monestime; Rudolph "Rudy" Moise, a doctor, lawyer and repeat congressional candidate; cultural leader Marshall Davis; and civil rights lawyer Roderick Vereen. Republican Te Mayonna Brown, a self-described real estate developer and pro-MAGA conservative, also qualified. Completing the ballot are Andy Daro, a North Bay Village Commissioner running with no party affiliation, and write-in candidate Patricia Gonzalez. The primary election is scheduled for August 18, with the general election in November.

cards.headline: Five Black candidates and Debbie Wasserman Schultz compete for Florida's 20th Congressional District
cards.teaser: Debbie Wasserman Schultz is now the only White candidate in a crowded Democratic Primary race for Florida's 20th Congressional District, a seat that has traditionally been represented by Black candidates.
cards.body:
Four Black candidates have qualified for the Democratic Primary in Florida's 20th Congressional District, joined by Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the longest-serving Democrat in Florida's congressional delegation and the only White candidate in the race. Other candidates include Luther Campbell, a rapper and community leader who was the frontman for 2 Live Crew, former U.S. Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness, and progressive activist Elijah Manley. Since the early 1990s, District 20 has had a Black-majority population, but a new map approved by Gov. Ron DeSantis changed that demographic composition. Cherfilus-McCormick resigned in April to avoid a possible expulsion vote after an Ethics investigation found she broke House rules 25 times. She is also under federal investigation for allegedly directing over $5 million in federal disaster funds to her 2021 campaign. Holness previously ran against Cherfilus-McCormick in the last Democratic Primary for this seat and lost by just five votes. Manley has raised the most money among those challenging Wasserman Schultz.

Wasserman Schultz has faced criticism for running in a seat traditionally represented by Black candidates, with Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried addressing these concerns to the Miami Herald. The race has seen concerns about possible antisemitism. Holness was accused of questioning whether Jews were trying to win all the region's congressional seats, though he denies the statement. Wasserman Schultz is Jewish. For the Republicans, Lateresa "LA" Jones, Rod Joseph, Brent Anderson, and nurse Carla Spalding have qualified, along with independent candidate Kedner Maxime. The Democratic Primary will likely decide the next representative, as the area is a Democratic stronghold with approximately 68 percent voting for Harris for President. Since there is no runoff, the Democratic Primary winner will likely serve the next two years.

cards.headline: Northeast Florida legislative seats fill out with some incumbents elected unopposed
cards.teaser: Now that qualifying has concluded in Northeast Florida Senate and House races, there is clarity on who residents of Nassau, Duval and Clay Counties will see on ballots in August and November.
cards.body:
In the race to replace term-limited Wyman Duggan, Jacksonville City Councilman Terrance Freeman is the sole Republican candidate with roughly $445,000 raised between his campaign and committee accounts. Democrat Ben Sandlin, who ran against Duggan in 2024, qualified again for the seat covering much of southern Duval County, which has a GOP registration advantage. In HD 13, two Democrats qualified to replace departing Angie Nixon: former Senate Democratic Leader Audrey Gibson and former state House hopeful Leslie Scott Jean-Bart will face off in August. Gibson has about $15,000 on hand, with donors including former state Sen. Tony Hill and Adam Hollingsworth, the former Chief of Staff for Rick Scott when he was Governor and John Peyton when he was Jacksonville Mayor. Write-in Brice Galliard has qualified, meaning only Democrats can vote in August's Primary.

Some incumbents were re-elected without opposition. In SD 4, HD 11 and HD 16, Republican Sen. Clay Yarborough, House Speaker-designate Sam Garrison and Rep. Kiyan Michael were re-elected without opposition.

cards.headline: Florida Rep. Paula Stark fails to qualify for re-election, giving Democrats early win in HD 47
cards.teaser: Paula Stark has appeared to not qualify for re-election in House District 47, meaning Democrats would win back a blue seat in a traditionally Democratic district covering St. Cloud, east Kissimmee and a small portion of Orange County.
cards.body:
Rep. Paula Stark has failed to qualify for re-election in House District 47, clearing the field for Democrats to reclaim the traditionally blue seat. The only qualifying candidates are Democrats Jorge Figueroa and Anthony Nieves. Figueroa serves as President of the Puerto Rican Chamber of Commerce of Central Florida, while Nieves is a former state investigator. Since both candidates are from the same party, all registered voters regardless of party affiliation will be able to vote in the August 18 Primary.

Stark's tenure in office was undermined by persistent campaign finance problems. Last year, the Friends of Paula political committee, run by Stark's boyfriend, was shut down by the state for failing to pay more than $16,000 in fines stemming from late campaign finance reports in 2023. Despite these issues, Stark won election in 2022 on a red wave and received an endorsement from the Orlando Sentinel. In Tallahassee, she demonstrated independence from the GOP party line, notably voting as one of only two Republicans against a bill banning local governments from supporting parades, festivals and activities celebrating diversity, equality and inclusion. Critics worried the legislation would harm events such as Pride parades and St. Patrick's Day parades.

hero.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office identifies rookie deputy who tackled golf course suspect
hero.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office has identified a rookie deputy who was seen tackling a suspect on a golf course.

"He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others—all with humility and determination," Armstead said. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime Youth of the Year judge, noted that Enrique distinguished himself throughout the selection process. "From the start, Enrique stood out. Thanks to his hard work—and all those who support him—we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year," Leonard said. "I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community."

Enrique's family has expressed deep gratitude for the opportunities he has received. His parents credited their faith and the support of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County in helping their son develop as both a leader and a person. The Youth of the Year program represents Boys & Girls Clubs of America's premier recognition for teenagers who serve as role models and change-makers in their communities. cards.headline: Daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death suit against trucker and freight broker
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian, whose mother was killed in an August 2025 crash in St. Lucie County, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the truck driver, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Faniola Joseph, 37, Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were traveling for work in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three people in the minivan were killed. Singh worked for White Hawk Carriers, a company with a troubling safety record. Joseph's only child, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices. Angeline is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart law firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer.

Bello argues the case is strengthened by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. That ruling involved the same broker named in Angeline's case. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warns they may reopen under another name. Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in person in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls.

The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through rare close-up encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman explains that the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex ecosystem models dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, setting it apart from most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said, noting that more species are housed here than in many larger exhibits. The Atlantic coral reef exhibit is the centerpiece, a sprawling tank recreating one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating intricate relationships between organisms, including a four-inch barracuda.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, with visitors likely encountering animals they have never seen before. The facility operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station to raise public awareness about ocean threats while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced through live displays. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, the aquarium is open to the public year-round. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year.

hero.headline: Indian River County could lose $50 million under property tax amendment on November ballot
hero.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach on Friday morning to address concerns about a property tax amendment heading to voters this November. The amendment would increase the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. County officials and community leaders expressed alarm over the potential financial impact, with projections showing the county could lose approximately $50 million in funding by 2028 from its roughly $597 million budget.

Laura Moss, vice chair of the Indian River County Commission, organized the meeting to bring together neighbors and community leaders to discuss the amendment's implications. Moss criticized the state's approach, saying "The state is going to dictate to the local governments how we fund whatever it is we fund. Every county is different. We fund what the community wants." Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called the amendment "an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy" and emphasized that the projected revenue loss represents a substantial portion of the county's annual budget. For a smaller county like Indian River, he noted, such a reduction could prove devastating to essential services.

The potential impact on emergency services is particularly concerning. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, stated that fire rescue could lose between $15 to $20 million from its $70 million budget, since about 79.1 percent of the department's funding comes from ad valorem taxes. The budget shortfall could prevent the development of three projected fire stations. Lunceford emphasized there is no realistic way to absorb such a large loss without cutting into law enforcement and first responder services that the community depends on.

Rather than a genuine tax cut for residents, Lunceford characterized the amendment as a tax shift that would place financial burdens elsewhere. To compensate for lost homestead exemption revenue, the county may need to increase taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties or raise impact fees and utility fees. Lunceford warned that increasing taxes on businesses ultimately increases costs for everyone, as higher business taxes translate to higher prices for consumers. The amendment represents what Moss called "a war on local government" by the state, highlighting the tension between Tallahassee's policy decisions and local governments' ability to fund the services their communities require.
